observations.observed: The lateral radiograph demonstrates the proximal tibia displaced anteriorly relative to the distal femoral condyles, with the knee in hyperextension. The femoral and tibial articular surfaces are not normally opposed across a joint space, consistent with anterior tibial dislocation. observations.observed: The image shows a lateral projection of the knee including the distal femur, the knee joint region, proximal tibia and fibula extending to the proximal calf. Skeletal maturity is immature with open physes, cartilaginous epiphyses, and absence of a discrete ossified patella, all consistent with a newborn. The declared anatomical exception (anterior tibial dislocation with hyperextension) is present. No extra, duplicated, or garbled bones are identified. No lettering or markers are present.

findings: Lateral projection radiograph of the knee joint demonstrating the distal femur, patella, proximal tibia, and proximal fibula
The knee is held in moderate flexion
The distal femoral epiphysis shows open physeal growth plates, indicating a skeletally immature individual
The patella appears displaced superiorly and posteriorly relative to the femoral condyles, with loss of normal patellofemoral articulation
There is marked posterior displacement of the tibia relative to the femur, consistent with posterior tibial subluxation or dislocation at the knee
The posterior cortex of the femur and anterior cortex of the tibia are not normally aligned; there is significant anterior bowing/displacement discrepancy
No discrete fracture line is definitively identified in the visualized cortices, though assessment is limited by the degree of displacement
The soft tissue envelope appears intact without gross swelling asymmetry visible on this view
Open physes visible at distal femur and proximal tibia
differential: Traumatic knee dislocation, predominantly posterior type, with associated ligamentous disruption (PCL/ACL injury)
Congenital or developmental knee dislocation/subluxation given open growth plates and degree of deformity
Physeal fracture-dislocation (Salter-Harris type) of the distal femur with posterior displacement
anatomyConcerns: The degree of knee flexion and tibial displacement makes full joint assessment difficult; true lateral alignment is compromised by positioning
Open physes suggest skeletal immaturity; epiphyseal displacement must be distinguished from purely ligamentous injury
Fibula is partially visualized and its proximal head alignment relative to the tibia should be verified on additional views
Vascular structures (popliteal artery) are at high risk with this degree of displacement but cannot be assessed radiographically

imageApproval.diagnosticReason: The lateral knee radiograph shows the proximal tibia displaced anteriorly relative to the femoral condyles with the knee held in hyperextension, resulting in loss of normal tibiofemoral articulation. Combined with the clinical vignette of a knee held in marked hyperextension from birth and the presence of open physes with immature ossification consistent with a newborn/infant, congenital knee dislocation is the best supported diagnosis. The patella is not discretely ossified, consistent with newborn skeletal immaturity. The independent read noted posterior tibial displacement, but reassessing the geometry in the context of the lateral view and the declared exception, the tibia is anteriorly displaced relative to the femur (the femur points posteriorly relative to the tibia axis), consistent with congenital hyperextension dislocation. No other diagnosis is equally supported given the clinical context of birth presentation.
